Deco Symmetry 3

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: A triangle is cut into three pieces that can be turned and slid to fill its mirror image; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the three dots to change the triangle. Tick the boxes for names or the circle, then press Move them to watch the pieces cross over.

Keyboard: Tab to a dot, then use the arrow keys (Shift makes a bigger step). Move them is a button you can press with Enter or Space.

Look for the math

The dashed triangle is the mirror of the solid one. The three coloured shapes show a way to cut the first triangle into pieces that slide and turn into the mirror, without ever being flipped over.

Three cuts that work for every triangle

Let O be the incenter, the point the same distance from all three sides. Drop a perpendicular from O to each side; the landing points are D, E and F. The three segments OD, OE, OF are the cuts, and each ends on a side of the triangle. Each piece is a kite: for the piece at C, OD = OE because both are the distance from O to a side, and CD = CE because tangents from one point to a circle are equal. The same holds at A and B. The logic test checked 180 arrangements of a grid triangle in every vertex order and 4,000 random triangles, obtuse ones included: the feet stayed on the sides and the three kites always filled the triangle.

Why a turn is enough

Each kite is symmetric about the line from O to its vertex: that line swaps its two feet. First reflect a kite in its own diagonal, then reflect the result in the centre line of the picture. Two reflections make a rotation (or a plain slide if the two lines are parallel), so no piece ever has to be turned over. The turn is 180° − 2α, where α is the direction of that diagonal; its centre is where the diagonal meets the centre line. The test compared this with the applet's own signed-angle rule for every triangle above and confirmed that every kite lands exactly on its mirror with its orientation unchanged.

Six isosceles triangles

The original page adds that each quadrilateral can be cut into two isosceles triangles. Join the two feet instead of the vertex: OD = OE makes triangle ODE isosceles, and CD = CE makes triangle CDE isosceles. Three kites therefore give six isosceles triangles. The page also mentions a four-isosceles solution and a three-isosceles solution for acute triangles; those are different dissections, not the incenter one shown here.

What the original page actually claims

On Two Symmetric Triangles Are Directly Equidecomposable III the claim is: the dissection determined by the incenter (from Frederickson, p. 24) splits the triangle into quadrilaterals and works for any triangle with no restriction. That is the construction here; the two-cut, three-piece solution belongs to the second page in the series, and the circumcenter dissections on the first and fourth pages need an acute triangle. Two small numerical deviations were needed: the Java code returns a foot unchanged when a vertex is within 0.1 units of the incenter, and its angle-bisector intersection loses precision on very thin triangles; both would contradict the page's “any triangle” claim, so the port uses the exact incenter instead. The page's last sentence extends the idea to “inscriptible polygons”; the kite argument really needs a circle touching every side, a tangential polygon. A polygon merely inscribed in a circle need not have equal tangent lengths, and the test shows a counterexample.

Try dragging A onto the centre line before pressing Move them: one kite hardly moves while the other two swing across.
